Yet for all the progress in what these systems can do, comparatively little attention has been paid to how, and under what conditions, they break. This paper attempts to fill part of that gap. Drawing on over forty published works from 2020 through early 2025, I propose a four-dimensional taxonomy of LLM agent failure modes, organized around the core functional modules present in most agentic architectures: reasoning and planning, tool use and action execution, memory and context management, and multi-agent orchestration. For each dimension, I provide formal definitions of specific failure classes, describe triggering conditions, and supply concrete illustrative examples grounded in the empirical literature. I also introduce the Agent Robustness Evaluation Protocol (AREP)-a lightweight, framework-agnostic robustness evaluation methodology intended to surface latent failure risks before deployment rather than after. The paper concludes with seven practitioner recommendations for building agentic systems that are not merely capable, but meaningfully robust and reliable.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6572478\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7433399\", \"title\": [\"When Agentic AI Breaks Software Quality Assurance: Failure Modes, Reliability Risks, and Governance Strategies for Autonomous Testing Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is changing software quality assurance from a predominantly human-directed activity into an increasingly autonomous process in which AI systems can generate tests, execute programs, interpret failures, modify test suites, and iteratively refine their actions. While these capabilities promise substantial improvements in testing speed, coverage, and engineering productivity, they also introduce a distinct class of quality risks. An autonomous testing agent can produce a technically executable test that encodes an incorrect assumption, misinterpret a failure, optimize for coverage rather than meaningful defect detection, or repeatedly reinforce an erroneous testing strategy. This article examines these risks through an integrative review of research on large language models (LLMs), automated software testing, AI-assisted software engineering, and AI governance. The analysis identifies six interconnected failure modes: erroneous test generation, defective test oracles, autonomous error propagation, coverage-driven quality illusion, contextual and repository misunderstanding, and governance and accountability failure. The article argues that the central challenge is not simply whether AI can generate valid tests, but whether autonomous testing systems can maintain trustworthy quality judgments under uncertainty. Drawing on empirical evidence from recent studies of ChatGPT, LLM-based test generation, TestGen-LLM, and software-engineering agents, the article proposes a risk-based governance model built around bounded autonomy, independent verification, traceability, human checkpoints, continuous monitoring, and explicit escalation mechanisms. The findings suggest that enterprise adoption should treat agentic testing as a controlled socio-technical system rather than a replacement for software quality expertise.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7433399\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/s10458-008-9067-4\", \"title\": [\"Goals in conflict: semantic foundations of goals in agent programming\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/s10458-008-9067-4\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2008, 10, 16]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/vkqk1326\", \"title\": [\"Safety Shields, an Automated Failure Handling Mechanism for BDI Agents\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The Belief Desire Intention model is a widely used architecture for developing rational agents. Because of its expressiveness, the task of programming a BDI agent can be challenging, especially when applied to safety-critical scenarios. In such scenarios, it is important to provide a safeguard for the critical behaviour of the agent. In this paper, we summarise how to extend the agent's reasoning cycle in the BDI model with safety shields. A safety shield works as a sandbox for the agents' plans that is enforced at runtime so that the agent behaves according to a safety formal specification. A runtime monitor is automatically synthesised from a shield to detect any failure that is within the scope of the shielded plan.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/vkqk1326\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2022, 5, 9]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "d1c43a7b7f153683fb63c81772a07b828f474b1c1c9637888f0cffe6566daca2", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "obedience_limits", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6572478", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7433399", "doi:10.1007/s10458-008-9067-4", "doi:10.65109/vkqk1326"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6572478", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7433399", "https://doi.org/10.1007/s10458-008-9067-4", "https://doi.org/10.65109/vkqk1326"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
